title: Backtracking
summary: Build candidate answers one choice at a time, undo each choice after exploring it, and prune branches that cannot succeed.
lesson:
How it works
- Backtracking is depth-first search over a tree of partial solutions. Each level makes one choice, recurses, then undoes the choice before trying the next option.
- A path that reaches a complete, valid state is recorded; a path that can no longer succeed is abandoned immediately.
- The running time is usually exponential in the worst case, so pruning decides how fast it is in practice.

When to reach for it
- The question asks for all combinations, subsets, permutations, or arrangements that satisfy a rule.
- You must decide whether a path exists through a grid or graph without reusing cells.
- The input is small enough that an exponential search is acceptable.

Common patterns
- Choose, explore, unchoose: append to a shared list, recurse, then remove the last element.
- Start index: pass the position to continue from so the same combination is not generated in another order.
- Visited marking: mark a cell before recursing and restore it afterward so other paths may use it.
- Pruning: sort the options so a branch can stop as soon as the remaining options are too large.

Pitfalls
- Forgetting to undo a choice, which leaks state into sibling branches.
- Saving a reference to the shared working list instead of a copy when recording an answer.
- Producing duplicate answers that differ only in order.
- Recursion depth grows with the length of a path; keep it bounded by the input size.
